doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
title: Horn players, doo wop, the Beatles and support for jazz
summary: Horn players could not join doo wop groups; he criticizes simple rock but praises the Beatles and laments weak support for jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well yeah and I guess it would be hardest on all the horn players.
Because a rhythm section player could choose to say well all right I’m going to play with a doo wop group, but the horn players were like — they don’t even have the opportunity.
Well if you notice, like trombonists and trumpets, see saxophones sure, they could play the tenor and lay on their back.
Walk the bar and all that stuff.

Yeah. So it was a little detrimental and I just ignored them, I didn’t even listen. Like all those tunes from the Doo Wop tunes, they’re good tunes too. I can enjoy them now. But then they were just pushing us out of work. So I just, as far as I was concerned, and then some of them they didn’t do the right chords or melody line. There was one group that sang [sings] I told every little star/just how sweet I think you are/why haven’t I told you. Then on the bridge they completely screwed it up. They changed the bridge. So I guess they didn’t know it. Because you know many times people, especially if you were playing by ear, the bridge is difficult. So you get to that middle part and you say uh oh. But that was just one of the things. And you’d listen to them and then say oh my God, they’re mutilating the melody, the chord changes are so basic, and after you’re listening — you know you’re listening to Oscar Peterson and Bud Powell and Wynton Kelly — you’re listening to all these guys and Shearing, oh. And so it’s seemed so simple,

simplistic you know. And then when they started the Beatles, now the Beatles, when you study their music they are something else. They’ve got standards out. They’ve got tunes that you can play for anybody. “Michelle.” [sings] Yesterday [scats] beautiful you know? “Norwegian Wood.” Oh man. But then there’s a lot of these other groups, but what they had, the mile high amplifiers and the roar of sound that practically knocks you over, and they’re prancing on the stage, even breaking up instruments on the stage you know. So it depended on your musicianship you know. The more you know the tougher it is to go on. But then it makes money. See and your promoters, see the promoters, they could do more for jazz, because jazz is our American classical music see. But we can’t get the support. We can’t get the financial support that European classical music gets or that the things like the Rolling Stones. They draw. When they go out they draw such huge crowds. And the tickets cost a bundle. But see we can’t get that kind of support. You can have a small following, people that come in, they enjoy what you do.
